title: Performance determinants in trail-running races of different distances
authors: Pastor FS, Besson T, Varesco G, Parent A, Fanget M, Koral J, et al.
journal: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
population: Trail runners entered in UTMB-week races (SHORT <55 km, MEDIUM 101 km, LONG >145 km) tested before the race
findings: 75 trail runners recruited; 24 finished SHORT, 16 MEDIUM and 14 LONG.
SHORT performance was explained by VO2max and lipid utilisation at 10 km/h (r2 = .825, P < .001).
MEDIUM (101 km) performance was determined by VO2max, maximal isometric strength and body fat percentage (r2 = .917, P < .001).
A linear model could not be applied in LONG (>145 km), but performance correlated with peak velocity in the incremental test.
limitations: Small samples per distance, finishers only (survivor bias), one event and set of conditions; lab-based predictors the engine cannot measure.
implications: Include a strength-maintenance component (knee extensor and plantar flexor force work) in plans for about 100 km and longer trail goals, since maximal isometric strength was a determinant at 101 km.
Use aerobic capacity (a VO2max proxy) as a limiter for 50 to 100 km goals; for over 145 km treat peak speed as a weak correlate only.
No strength dose is justified by this study; a dose needs another source.

verification.notes: Crossref (2022-06-01, 11 authors, last author Millet) and Europe PMC abstract re-fetched; all numbers confirmed.
